payload.body: Carrier is a human-made signal-engineering construct: a high-frequency waveform selected and sustained to bear an information-bearing signal across a channel. Three parameters carve it: (1) frequency selection: a carrier frequency is chosen outside the information bandwidth and maintained stable by oscillators and control loops; (2) modulation coupling: information is impressed on the carrier via amplitude, frequency, or phase modulation, making the carrier the physical substrate that carries the message; (3) channel fit: the carrier’s spectral occupancy, power, and propagation characteristics are matched to the transmission medium and receiver. Carriers persist through engineering standards, hardware implementations, and operational practice: oscillators generate them, transmitters broadcast them, receivers lock to them, and protocols specify their use. [formal: carrier | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: Phonetics is a human-made discipline of linguistics that studies the physical properties of speech sounds, as distinct from their systemic function within a particular language. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) domain: the object is the speech sound as a physical event — articulation (the configuration and movement of the articulators in producing it), acoustics (the pressure wave it generates), and perception (its auditory detection); the domain's boundary is the physical signal itself — the systemic organization of sound units into inventories and rules belongs to phonology, as the board's accepted morphology carve already assigns sound structure to phonology at the word's domain boundary; (2) method: analysis proceeds by measurement and cross-linguistic description — articulatory geometry, acoustic values such as formants and spectrograms, and perceptual classification — rather than by the contrastive inventory of any single language; (3) codification: findings are fixed in a shared apparatus independent of any one language — the International Phonetic Alphabet and its conventions, articulatory taxonomies (consonants by place and manner of articulation), and acoustic norms — which give phonetics its stable, reusable descriptive form. Phonetics persists as a discipline: it is taught as a field of linguistics, its categories (formant, place and manner of articulation, phoneme's physical realization) form the stable vocabulary of speech description across languages, and its apparatus is operationalized in speech synthesis and recognition, forensic phonetics, and the clinical assessment of speech. payload.body: Phonology is a human-made discipline of linguistics that studies the sound systems of languages: what sounds a language has, which of them are distinctive, and the rules governing how they combine, co-occur, and vary in speech. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) domain — the object is the sound structure of a language at and below the level of the word: the inventory of distinctive sound units (the phoneme system), their contextual variants (allophones), and the constraints and rules on their combinations (phonotactics, assimilation, stress, tone); the domain's boundaries are set by the level of analysis — the physical and perceptual description of speech sounds belongs to phonetics, the decomposition of words into morphemes belongs to morphology, and meaning belongs to semantics; (2) method — analysis proceeds by contrasting minimal pairs to isolate the distinctive units of a language, by describing the phonetic variants that surface in specific contexts, and by stating the rules that map an underlying representation onto its surface form; (3) codification — findings are fixed as phonemic inventories, phonotactic constraints, and rule statements that differ per language but share a stable descriptive form. Phonology persists as a discipline: it is taught as a field of linguistics, its categories (phoneme, allophone, phonotactics, stress, tone) form the stable vocabulary of grammatical description across languages, and its methods are operationalized in dictionaries, speech technology, and language documentation. [formal: phonologia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: An allophone is a human-made phonological category — the contextual variant of a phoneme: the particular surface realization that a language's phonology assigns to a phoneme in a specific phonetic environment, without changing word meaning. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) identity anchoring — every allophone is indexed to a phoneme; it is that phoneme's surface form in a given context, so the allophone set of a language is the variant set of its phoneme inventory (in English, /p/ is realized as aspirated [pʰ] at the start of a stressed syllable, as in 'pin', and as unaspirated [p] after /s/, as in 'spin'); (2) distribution — the allophones of a phoneme occur in complementary distribution, their environments not overlapping, which is exactly what separates a predictable variant from a contrastive phonemic pair; free variation, where two variants share an environment without changing meaning, is the boundary case the category is carved against; (3) predictability — the variant is determined by environment according to the language's phonological rules and can be predicted from context, unlike phonemic choice, which is selected for meaning. The boundary with phonetics is set by the level of analysis: the physical and auditory description of the variant belongs to phonetics; what is carved here is the phonological category of the variant within a language's sound system. The codification mechanism is the transcription convention itself: the phoneme is written in slashes /p/ and its allophonic realizations in square brackets [pʰ], so the distinction is carried in every phonological description. Allophones persist as a discipline's standing category: taught in phonology curricula, fixed in the phonemic inventories and rule statements of language description, and operationalized in speech technology and language documentation. [formal: allophonum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

payload.scope: A human-made science — the formal study of communication and control in animals and machines — built to persist as the discipline Wiener founded in 1948, maintained through its textbooks, its engineering applications, and its theoretical descendants.

payload.body: Cybernetics is a human-made science — the study of communication and control in animals and machines, in Wiener's own subtitle. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) subject matter — cybernetics addresses communication and control systems wherever they occur: the nervous system, the thermostat, the feedback amplifier, the fire-control radar; its core concept is feedback — the correction of a system's behavior by an error signal — and it treats biological and mechanical controllers as instances of one formal kind, so 'communication' and 'control' name the same underlying mechanism; (2) founding and method — founded in Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics: Or Concerning Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine (1948), the discipline arose from the wartime convergence of information theory, physiology, statistics, and engineering practice, and its method is the mathematical modeling of feedback loops, stability, and noise; (3) transmission — cybernetics persists as a discipline: textbooks and journals (from von Foerster's Kybernetik onward), engineering practice (automatic control, servomechanisms, signal processing), and its theoretical descendants — systems theory, second-order cybernetics (Maturana, Varela, von Foerster), and the feedback vocabulary that fields as distant as economics and ecology still borrow. Boundaries: it is not information theory (the source it drew on), not engineering control theory (the sibling it fed), and not systems theory (the descendant that generalized it) — cybernetics is the feedback-based study of communication and control spanning living and machine. [formal: kybernetike | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.35]

payload.body: Phonotactics is a human-made phonological category — the set of rules that govern which sound combinations are permissible in a language and where they may occur. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) constraint scope: the object is the inventory of permissible phoneme sequences in a language, including onsets (initial consonant clusters), codas (final consonant clusters), and syllable structure — for example, English permits /str-/ at word onset but not /ŋ-/ or /vn-/; Japanese restricts syllable structure to (C)V, allowing at most a single consonant-vowel nucleus with optional coda; (2) language-relativity: what counts as permissible in one language may be impossible in another, since the phonotactic constraints of each language form a distinct system that speakers internalize as unconscious knowledge — a sequence that is a well-formed word in one language may be impossible or trigger repair strategies in another; (3) descriptive form: phonotactics is expressed as constraints on phoneme sequences, typically stated as production rules, feature-based restrictions, or probabilistic models that map which transitions between phonemes are licensed in which positions. Phonotactics persists as a descriptive tool: it is taught as part of phonological analysis, codified in dictionaries that include phonetic transcriptions, and operationalized in speech synthesis, speech recognition, and language documentation to constrain the generative space of possible word forms.

payload.body: Phonotactics is a human-made phonological category — the set of rules that govern which sound combinations are permissible in a language and where they may occur. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) constraint scope: the object is the inventory of permissible phoneme sequences in a language, including onsets (initial consonant clusters), codas (final consonant clusters), and syllable structure — for example, English permits /str-/ at word onset but not /ŋ-/ or /vn-/; Japanese restricts syllable structure to (C)V, allowing at most a single consonant-vowel nucleus with optional coda; (2) language-relativity: what counts as permissible in one language may be impossible in another, since the phonotactic constraints of each language form a distinct system that speakers internalize as unconscious knowledge — a sequence that is a well-formed word in one language may be impossible or trigger repair strategies in another; (3) descriptive form: phonotactics is expressed as constraints on phoneme sequences, typically stated as production rules, feature-based restrictions, or probabilistic models that map which transitions between phonemes are licensed in which positions. Phonotactics persists as a descriptive tool: it is taught as part of phonological analysis, codified in dictionaries that include phonetic transcriptions, and operationalized in speech synthesis, speech recognition, and language documentation to constrain the generative space of possible word forms. [formal: phonotactica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: A distinctive feature is a human-made phonological category — a valued property of a speech sound used to characterize and distinguish the phonemes of a language: the smallest contrastive attribute by which one phoneme is separated from another (voicing separates /p/ from /b/; place of articulation separates /p/ from /t/ from /k/). Three parameters carve the construct: (1) contrastive role — the feature is the unit of phonemic contrast: two phonemes of a language are distinct because they differ in at least one distinctive feature, and a phoneme's identity is the complete bundle of its feature values (the feature matrix: /p/ is [voiceless, bilabial, stop]; /b/ is [voiced, bilabial, stop]), so a language's phoneme inventory is an inventory of distinct feature bundles; (2) valued structure — features come in classes (laryngeal: voicing; oral cavity: place, manner; root: nasality), each valued, binary (+/−) or multi-valued (place = bilabial, labiodental, alveolar, postalveolar, velar, uvular, ...; manner = stop, fricative, nasal, lateral, approximant), and the theory organizes the classes into hierarchies (feature geometry: laryngeal, oral-cavity, and root nodes with place and manner branches); (3) codification — conventions are fixed in the phonological literature (the standard feature lists of generative phonology; feature geometry), in the IPA's classification, and in operational formalisms — feature-based phonotactic restrictions, feature-based rule systems, and computational phonology. The distinctive feature persists as a tool of analysis: it is taught as a core apparatus of phonology, published in standard textbooks and handbooks, and operationalized in feature-based phonotactic constraints, dictionary phonetic transcription, and speech technology. [formal: differentia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.note: Pinned sense: the distinctive feature as the valued contrastive property that fixes a phoneme's identity (target's filed definition: a phoneme's identity is the complete bundle of its feature values). REMOVAL TEST (does X stop operating if Y is removed now?): the accepted phoneme definition fixes the phoneme as the smallest abstract unit of sound such that substitution changes word meaning — and the mechanism of that substitution is precisely the feature: two phonemes are distinct because they differ in at least one distinctive feature, and the minimal pair works because /p/ and /b/ differ in [±voice]. Remove the features and the units cannot contrast: without contrastive attributes a sound unit cannot be separated from its neighbors, the minimal-pair mechanism collapses, and the construct stops operating as a phoneme. This is a mechanism dependency, not a kind appeal: the feature is the means by which the phoneme distinguishes, not a category the phoneme belongs to. Sense note: the target is the phonological distinctive feature, not the 'feature' entry, whose accepted definition fixes the data-engineering sense.

REMOVAL TEST (does X stop operating if Y is removed now?): phonotactic constraints act on phoneme sequences — onsets, codas, and syllable structure are all patterns over the phoneme inventory. Remove the phoneme (the unit the constraints operate on) and the constraints lose their object: permissible and forbidden patterns are no longer patterns of phonological units but bare patterning of sound, and the system stops operating as phonotactics. This is an object dependency, not chronology: phonotactics DERIVED_FROM phonology is already accepted (the discipline came first), but the operating object of the constraints is the phoneme — it is removing the phoneme, not the discipline, that stops the constraints operating.

In the target's accepted definition the phoneme's operating mechanism is the minimal-pair criterion: the smallest abstract unit of sound such that substitution changes meaning. Distinctive features appear as a descriptive parameter of how phonemes DIFFER (voicing, place, manner), not as an input whose removal stops the construct operating. Removal test: remove the concept of distinctive feature and the minimal-pair mechanism still identifies and separates phonemes by distribution and contrastive substitution — the feature matrix is a later, optional formalization (Halle–Studdard 1953; Chomsky–Halle 1968) of a contrastivity that operates without it. The note's core claim that "the mechanism of that substitution is precisely the feature" is false: minimal pairs work by contrastive substitution, not by feature values. A descriptive/analytic lens is not an operating dependency; the claim is coherent but fails the removal test on the defined sense. STRIKE.

Pinned sense: segment as bounded speech sound unit in phonological analysis (per segment's filing: bounded spans of phonetic material treated as single units). In standard phonological usage, 'segment' is the standing class of the discrete units of segmental phonology — consonants and vowels, contrasted with suprasegmental features — and a phoneme is the abstract, contrastive member of that class: 'consonant phonemes' and 'vowel phonemes' are precisely segments, and a syllable is counted by its segments. A competent phonologist calls a phoneme 'a segment' (an abstract one). Nearest-kind (Laws 9/11e): no accepted intermediate kind sits between phoneme and segment on this board (no phonological-unit, no suprasegmental/prosody kind entry); the accepted phoneme INSTANCE_OF unit is a separate, broader parent, not a ladder rung that segment skips — segment is the more specific kind for phonological material. Not the struck category-to-discipline leap (segment is a co-category inside phonology, not the discipline), and not a property leap: segment is a class of units defined by contrast with suprasegmental features, independently of phoneme, and phoneme falls under it. ADVANCE.

payload.name: suprasegment
payload.scope: A human-made phonological category mapping the prosodic properties of speech — stress, tone, length, intonation — onto features that span a stretch of segments rather than constituting single units of the sound stream, built to persist as the counterpart of segment in the standard segmental/suprasegmental analysis of sound systems.

payload.name: suprasegment
payload.scope: A human-made phonological category mapping the prosodic properties of speech — stress, tone, length, intonation — onto features that span a stretch of segments rather than constituting single units of the sound stream, built to persist as the counterpart of segment in the standard segmental/suprasegmental analysis of sound systems.

payload.body: A suprasegment is a human-made phonological category — the concept of a prosodic feature or unit that spans one or more segments rather than constituting a single unit of the sound stream: a property of a stretch of speech (a syllable, a word, a phrase) rather than of any one sound within it. It is the counterpart of segment in the standard dichotomy: segmental description covers the units of the stream (the consonant and vowel inventory), while suprasegmental description covers the properties distributed across those units. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the property that spans — the prosodic property a language exploits: stress (relative prominence within a word), tone (pitch contrast associated with a syllable or word), length (duration contrast), intonation (pitch movement over a phrase), rhythm (the patterning of prominent and non-prominent units); (2) the span — the sequence of segments across which the feature is distributed, typically a syllable or a word, so a suprasegment is identified by the stretch it covers and the property it carries across that stretch; (3) the system — the language's prosody, which fixes which suprasegmental contrasts are distinctive (stress distinguishes 'REcord' from 'reCORD' in English; tone distinguishes syllables in Mandarin; where a language lacks tonal contrast, pitch is not a distinctive suprasegment). Persistence mechanism: the conventions of phonological description — suprasegmental features are encoded in transcription (stress marks, tone diacritics, length marks, pitch contours), taught as the second half of the segmental/suprasegmental analysis in phonology courses, and operationalized in prosodic phonology, dictionary pronunciation, and speech synthesis. [formal: suprasegmentum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Pinned sense (Law 11d): distinctive-feature as the phonological category of contrastive attributes, i.e. 'the smallest contrastive attribute by which one phoneme is separated from another' — the UNIT OF PHONEMIC CONTRAST. Its accepted definition makes the contrastive role its first and defining parameter: a feature's identity IS its role in separating phonemes, and a phoneme's identity is the bundle of its feature values. Removal test (Law 8b): remove the concept of phoneme and 'phonemic contrast' loses its referent — there is no unit the feature is contrastive OF, no phoneme inventory to be an inventory of feature bundles, no feature matrix to fill, no feature-based phonotactic constraint to constrain. What survives is a mere valued property of speech sounds (a phonetic description), which is a different, more general construct. This is object-level, not a 'concept needs cognition' appeal: the feature is a theoretical description that requires the phoneme as its referent, unlike a practice that would persist without the label. Direction is consistent with the reverse edge I struck (phoneme does NOT depend on feature — the minimal-pair function stands without the feature apparatus), so the dependency is one-directional: feature -> phoneme. Historically it fits too — the phoneme (Trubetzkoy/Hjelmslev) predates the distinctive feature, which was built to characterize phonemes.

Law 8d — for whose sake was it built? The accepted definition says the distinctive feature 'persists as a tool of analysis: it is taught as a core apparatus of phonology, published in standard textbooks and handbooks, and operationalized in feature-based phonotactic constraints...'; its scope calls it 'the standard unit of contrast in phonological analysis.' The category was constructed for the sake of phonological analysis — servant (feature) points at master (phonology). The asymmetry the note draws is exactly right and is the test that separates SERVES from DEPENDS_ON: phonology operates without this category (the discipline is older and broader — distributional phonemics, non-feature formalisms, allophonic rule statements), so it is NOT a dependency; but the category exists for the discipline. Downstream operationalization in speech technology and dictionary transcription is application of a phonological tool, not a co-equal purpose — the tool was not built for speech technology any more than a scalpel is built for the operating room's billing system.

payload.body: An allomorph is a human-made morphological category — the phonologically or morphologically conditioned variant form of a morpheme, the surface realization by which an abstract morpheme is expressed in actual speech. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) conditioning — each variant is realized only in a specific phonological or morphological environment: the English plural morpheme surfaces as /s/ before voiceless obstruents (cats), as /z/ after voiced sounds (dogs), and as /iz/ after sibilants (boxes), and the past-tense morpheme appears as the suffix -ed or as the suppletive form went; (2) single identity — the variants are distributional alternants of ONE morpheme: they never contrast in meaning as separate morphemes would, and which variant occurs is predictable from context rather than freely chosen; (3) analyst level — an allomorph is a unit posited in description, not an entity speakers manipulate: speakers produce surface forms, and the category organizes those forms under a single morpheme. It persists as a stable category of the descriptive-morphology toolkit, maintained by documented alternation rules in grammars, by pedagogy, and by the reproducible distributional tests that separate allomorphy from free variation and from distinct morphemes. [formal: allomorphum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: The syllable is a human-made unit of phonological analysis: a bounded span of speech material organized around a sonority peak (nucleus) with dependent margins (onset and coda). Parameters: (1) the unit is delimited by a prominence peak — typically a vowel or syllabic sonorant — around which consonantal material is assigned to margins; (2) the assignment is constrained by the language's phonotactics (which consonant strings may open or close the span); (3) the unit functions as the carrier of stress, tone, and rhythm, and as the counting unit of meter. It is distinguished from the segment in that it is constituted by a structured sequence of segments rather than a single contrastive position, and from the word in that it is sublexical and freely reconstituted across morpheme boundaries. Persistence mechanism: the syllable tier of phonological theory, encoded in transcription conventions (syllable boundaries, moraic structure), prosodic analysis, and metrical practice, and taught as a standard unit of linguistic description. [formal: syllaba | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Agree with the challenge. The held 'unit' definition is the metrology sense: 'a standardized reference magnitude against which quantities are compared — the fixed point that turns raw comparison into measurement,' with parameters of quantity kind (length/mass/duration), reference (artifact, procedure, or physical constant), and authority (standards body/treaty/custom). The edge's pinned sense — 'the basic segmental unit of speech sound' — uses the constituent/element homonym of the polysemous word 'unit', which the held carve does not cover. A phoneme fails every carved parameter: it standardizes no quantity kind (it is an abstract class of speech sounds, not a magnitude), it is defined by minimal-pair distinction within a language rather than a reference artifact or constant, and no standards body maintains it. Law 11d: the judge judges the pinned sense against the target's accepted definition — the pinned sense must instantiate the held sense, not merely share a word with it. Family corroboration: every other accepted INSTANCE_OF into unit is a measurement magnitude (bel, decibel, neper). This is the homograph trap. The edge is a misclassification and should fall; if the map later wants a constituent-unit sense of 'unit', that is a distinct filing. ADVANCE (target falls).

payload.sense: The MORPHOLOGICAL paradigm: the complete set of inflected forms of a single lexeme arranged in the table of the grammar's inflectional slots — the conjugation/declension table (Latin amare: amo, amas, amat...; English ox: ox, oxen). A set of word-forms keyed to one lexeme, not a community's framework of assumptions.
payload.distinction: A concrete test against the existing holder (the Kuhnian shared framework): (1) KEY — the held paradigm is keyed to a COMMUNITY and a domain (it prescribes what counts as a valid problem/solution for practitioners); the morphological paradigm is keyed to a SINGLE LEXEME and its cells are word-forms. (2) INDEPENDENT CHANGE — the held paradigm changes when a rival framework resolves more anomalies (Kuhnian crisis and replacement; its persistence mechanism is education, peer review, professional societies); the morphological paradigm changes when a lexeme's inflection or the grammar's slot structure changes (English losing case inflection reshaped its noun paradigm tables while no community of practitioners changed framework; a community can shift its scientific paradigm without a single conjugation table moving). Each can change while the other stands still, so the constructs operate independently. (3) OPERABLE DIFFERENCE — the morphological paradigm is conjugatable: it has slots, cells, and a lexeme key, and a finite-state transducer can generate it; the held paradigm has none of these — it cannot be conjugated, has no cells, and is not a set of forms. (4) ETYMOLOGY — both senses descend from the Greek 'model/pattern' (paradeigma); the morphological sense is the older attested use (the model-word set displaying a verb's pattern in ancient grammars), the Kuhnian sense is a 20th-century metaphor from it. Same word, distinct constructs.

payload.body: Paradigm is a human-made morphological category — the complete set of formally related word-forms of a single lexeme, arranged in a systematic series that displays the inflectional slots the grammar assigns to that lexeme's class. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) unit of completeness: the paradigm is a set keyed to one lexeme — it collects every inflected form the grammar assigns to it (Latin amare yields amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant; English ox yields the set ox, oxen), so it is the full form-set, never a single form and never a cross-lexeme list; (2) systematic arrangement: the forms are ordered by the grammar's inflectional dimensions (person × number × tense × mood for verbs; case × number × gender for nouns), and that slot structure — the table — is itself the stable object: every lexeme of a given class fills the same slots, and comparing how classes fill the slots is how the grammar describes its own inflectional system; (3) regularity as a parameter of the table: the paradigm records which cells are rule-predictable (regular: English walked from walk) and which must be memorized (irregular: English go–went–gone, Latin sum–es–est), so paradigm shape and size vary by language, by class, and by individual lexeme and the variation is part of the description, not noise. Paradigms persist as the stable unit of inflectional description: conjugation and declension tables in grammars and language pedagogy, the paradigmatic axis of structural linguistics (Saussure: within a series, forms stand in paradigmatic relation as selectable equivalents), the unit of paradigm generation in computational morphology (finite-state transducers mapping one lexeme to all its inflected forms), and the comparative method's object for reconstructing the inflectional systems of ancestral languages (the PIE verb paradigm reconstructed from the Greek, Latin, and Sanskrit tables that still share its slot structure). [formal: paradigma | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

MISCLASSIFICATION of a unit as a part-whole constituent. I verified the board's own accepted edge pattern rather than the cited one in isolation: within morphology's ACCEPTED edges, the six CONTAINED items (inflection, derivation, compounding, affixation, infixation, tmesis) are all PROCESSES/sub-operations, while the single UNIT — morpheme, named in the morphology definition as a 'category' exactly as phoneme is named in the phonology definition — is related by morphology DEPENDS_ON morpheme, NOT morphology CONTAINS morpheme. The board has drawn and enforced a clean distinction: subfields (linguistics CONTAINS phonology) and processes (morphology CONTAINS inflection) are CONTAINED; abstract units/categories are related by DEPENDS_ON (morphology DEPENDS_ON morpheme; allophone DEPENDS_ON phonology, ACCEPTED). A phoneme is an abstract unit, not a process or subfield, so the consistent relation is a DEPENDS_ON, not a part-whole CONTAINS. Sibling consistency confirms it: allophone — the phoneme's direct sibling unit in the same 'categories (phoneme, allophone, ...)' list — is already ACCEPTED as allophone DEPENDS_ON phonology; making its sibling phoneme CONTAINED-by the discipline treats two co-defined units with different relation types, which the record cannot support. The note's appeal to 'named in the definition is the carve' proves too much: morpheme is likewise named in morphology's definition, yet the board chose DEPENDS_ON for it. STRIKE; the defensible edge is a DEPENDS_ON, which is a different filing.

Direction error — the whole-to-part arrow is reversed, and the note concedes it. The pinned claim: word-formation CONTAINS morphology, i.e. the discipline is a constituent part of the genus of processes. But the note's own argument runs the other way: 'Word-formation IS a part of morphology's domain of study — the morphology definition explicitly names word-formation in parameter 1.' A framework whose operations are the members of a genus is not itself a member/part of that genus: part-whole is asymmetric, and if morphology CONTAINS word-formation (the pending sibling edge g85bd24, which fits the board's accepted pattern of morphology CONTAINING named domain constituents), then word-formation CONTAINS morphology cannot also hold. The word-formation definition carves it as 'the genus comprising the processes' (members: compounding, affixation, infixation, tmesis — all INSTANCE_OF word-formation, accepted); morphology, which also covers the morpheme system and inflection, is strictly broader. The note never establishes morphology as a part of word-formation; it establishes the reverse. STRIKE.

Removal test passes on the pinned sense. Per the petitioning definition parameter 1, the paradigm is a set keyed to ONE lexeme — the single item whose full form-set it collects. Remove the lexeme and there is no subject whose forms could be arranged in the slot table: the set loses its organizing key and its identity (one lexeme's complete form-set) ceases to operate; what remains is at most an unordered list of word-forms. This is not identity-as-dependency (Law 8c): the lexeme is the abstract unit of meaning (dictionary headword), the paradigm is the human-made arrangement of its forms in the grammar's slot table — arrangement and key are distinct. The lexeme is a named input parameter in the definition, and the pattern matches the accepted edge one level up: morphology DEPENDS_ON lexeme (Seth, ACCEPTED, verified in graph) — the discipline and its unit of inflectional description share the substrate, and the unit cannot stand without the key.

Morphology is a discipline; stem is a linguistic unit studied by it. CONTAINS (Law 10) requires mereological composition — Y is literally a part inside X. A stem is not a part of the discipline of morphology any more than a note is a part of music theory. The morphology definition lists stem among its categories, but categories are conceptual organization, not physical parts. This conflates subject-matter with mereology. File INSTANCE_OF (stem INSTANCE_OF morphological-unit) or DEPENDS_ON instead.

payload.note: Pinned sense (Law 11d): phoneme per its accepted definition as the smallest abstract distinctive sound unit of a language; phonology per its accepted definition as the discipline that inventories the distinctive sounds of a language, its first domain parameter being 'the inventory of distinctive sound units (the phoneme system)'. DEPENDS_ON removal test (Law 8b): remove the phonological system — the distinctive-contrast inventory the discipline persists — and the phoneme loses the system in which its distinctiveness is constituted: without the inventory of distinctive contrasts, 'phoneme' is a label on sounds with no defined role, and the category ceases to operate as the unit it is. Not the generic conceptual-need appeal: the category's identity (smallest DISTINCTIVE unit) is constituted by the contrast system the discipline maintains. Family corroboration: the board's accepted sibling edge allophone DEPENDS_ON phonology — the phoneme's own co-listed sibling — runs unit-to-discipline on the same pattern; morphology's units likewise connect by DEPENDS_ON (morphology DEPENDS_ON morpheme, morphology DEPENDS_ON lexeme, both accepted), while CONTAINS is reserved for processes (morphology CONTAINS inflection) and subfields (linguistics CONTAINS phonology). Not SERVES: the phoneme is the discipline's constitutive unit, not a tool built for it.

Pinned sense (Law 11d): paradigm per its own petitioning definition as the complete set of inflected forms of a single lexeme arranged in the grammar's slot table — the stable unit of inflectional description. DEPENDS_ON removal test (Law 8b): remove morphology — the discipline that persists inflectional description (conjugation/declension tables in grammars and pedagogy, the paradigmatic axis of structural linguistics, paradigm generation in computational morphology, comparative reconstruction of inflectional systems, per the definition's own persistence paragraph) — and the paradigm loses every mechanism by which it persists as an object: no grammar to house the slot table, no transducer to generate it, no comparative method to reconstruct it. What remains are bare inflected forms as facts of the language, not an organized, persisted form-set. The paradigm as table-and-unit is a construct of the discipline's descriptive practice, the same pattern as the board's accepted allophone DEPENDS_ON phonology (a unit persisting within the discipline's framework). Not CONTAINS: the accepted discipline pattern reserves CONTAINS for processes (morphology CONTAINS inflection/derivation) and subfields (linguistics CONTAINS phonology); units connect by DEPENDS_ON (morphology DEPENDS_ON morpheme/lexeme; allophone DEPENDS_ON phonology). Complements, not replaces, the parallel paradigm DEPENDS_ON lexeme (the key and the framework are distinct removal targets).
